Cadge

KAJ · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To cadge to beg for or get something by asking, especially persistently and for small things.

He was known around the dorm for cadging snacks from anyone with a full pantry.

Worked Example

Too broke to buy his own, he spent the whole party cadging cigarettes from anyone who'd give him one.

Going around a party begging cigarettes off anyone is exactly cadging.

How Cadge Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

mooch

mooch: obtain something from others without paying

scrounge

scrounge: collect by begging or searching persistently

Antonyms

provide

provide: supply or give something needed

How Strong Is It? — borrow → cadge → sponge off

borrow vs. cadge

borrow vs. cadge: Borrow implies an expected, often single, return of the item; cadge implies a habitual pattern of getting small things without giving anything back.

sponge off vs. cadge

sponge off vs. cadge: To sponge off someone pushes the same habit further, implying ongoing dependence, while cadge can describe a single small ask, like one cigarette or one ride.

Build the Word

The pieces

Put it together

Put it together: Cadge is of uncertain origin, likely related to the dialect word cadger, a traveling peddler who went door to door -- a trade with a reputation for wheedling small favors along the way.

Use the root in a new word: cadger

Use the root in a new word: cadger: The related word cadger, an old dialect term for a traveling peddler, survives mostly in British regional speech and gives cadge its likely origin story.

Strength Check

Word Choice

Cadge is a casual, slightly disapproving word, almost always used for small, repeated asks -- a cigarette, a ride, a few dollars -- rather than one big favor.
